correctness.rationale: For each nonisotropic projective line L, its orthogonal complement is a distinct nonisotropic line and these lines pair without fixed points. Every ordered natural basis comes from one such ordered line pair and two nonzero scalars. Counting isotropic lines yields epsilon=0/2 for odd q and epsilon=1 for even q. Exactly the pair {ku,(ku)^perp} gives one-target graphs when B(u,u) is nonzero; no such pair exists when isotropic. The m=2 classification proves the sharp q=2 or split q=3 uniqueness boundary, with explicit algebras and full small-field enumeration. Two standalone exact programs check q=2,3,4,5 exhaustively in Gram matrices and generator vectors, and further extensions/prime fields; no finite test is represented as an infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The motivating 2026 survey asks for natural-basis counts and contains only an existence graph-change example. The inspected 2020 arXiv natural-families preprint and the 2021 bilinear classification give structural antecedents; neither inspected primary work gives the exact all-prime-power conditional graph distribution, natural-basis counts or sharp small-field unique-basis exceptions. The literal unrestricted statement of Corollary 2.7 in the inspected preprint fails in the two exhibited small fields. Historical-priority risk from unstated classical deductions is acknowledged.

value.rationale: The theorem exactly counts all natural bases modulo the natural equivalence, determines every possible graph and its probability over all finite fields, including even-characteristic extensions, and identifies the sharp conditions under which a fixed non-perfect algebra is unexpectedly natural-basis-rigid. Its q=2 and split q=3 examples give motivated, explicit boundaries of a published unrestricted uniqueness criterion and fully resolve the two-dimensional rank-one case of the survey’s natural-basis and graph questions.
